title: Give every feature switch its own bit

blocks.text: The billing service keeps each tenant's 48 feature switches in one `long`: feature n is on when bit n is set. Support has three tickets open. A tenant who bought the audit log (feature 42) also got single sign-on (feature 10). A cleanup job that switches off every trial feature switched some of them back on. And a tenant with only one feature of the "analytics" bundle was shown the whole bundle.
`FeatureMask` already builds sets of features and switches them on. Finish the three `TODO` methods in `src/main/java/practice/FeatureMask.java`:

items: `bit(feature)`: the set that holds one feature;
`disable(mask, features)`: the mask with those features switched off;
`hasAll(mask, features)`: whether every feature of the set is on.

cases.says: low-numbered features can be switched on, checked, and switched off
features 32 to 47 get bits of their own and never switch on a low-numbered feature
switching off a feature that is already off leaves it off
a check for several features is true only when every one of them is on

origin.section: Bit Operators Bind Looser Than ==, and an int Shift Counts Only to 31

concepts: (mask & set) != 0 asks whether any bit of the set is on and (mask & set) == set whether all are; mask & ~set clears the bits while ^ flips them.
An int shift uses only the low five bits of its distance and a long shift the low six, so 1 << 35 is 8 even when assigned to a long; the left operand must be a long.
